name: Kurdish (Kurmanji)
variety: Kurmanji (Northern Kurdish) as written in the Hawar Latin alphabet; standard based on the Botan-type dialects of southeastern Turkey, with notes on dialect variation
sources: Thackston, W. M. (2006). Kurmanji Kurdish: A Reference Grammar with Selected Readings. Harvard University (manuscript).
Bedir Khan, Djeladet and Lescot, Roger (1970). Grammaire kurde (dialecte kurmandji). Paris: Maisonneuve.
Blau, Joyce and Barak, Veysi (1999). Manuel de kurde: kurmanji. Paris: L'Harmattan.
Kahn, Margaret (1976). Borrowing and Variation in a Phonological Description of Kurdish. PhD dissertation, University of Michigan.
Haig, Geoffrey and Matras, Yaron (2002). Kurdish linguistics: a brief overview. Sprachtypologie und Universalienforschung 55(1).
Öpengin, Ergin and Haig, Geoffrey (2014). Regional variation in Kurmanji: a preliminary classification of dialects. Kurdish Studies 2(2).

Haig, Geoffrey and Öpengin, Ergin (2018). Kurmanji Kurdish in Turkey: structure, varieties and status. In Bulut (ed.), Linguistic Minorities in Turkey and Turkic-Speaking Minorities of the Periphery. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz.
McCarus, Ernest N. (2009). Kurdish. In Windfuhr (ed.), The Iranian Languages. London: Routledge.
contrasts: aspirated versus unaspirated voiceless stops and affricate: /pʰ p/, /tʰ t/, /kʰ k/, /tʃʰ tʃ/; together with the voiced series /b d ɡ dʒ/ a three-way laryngeal contrast; the Hawar alphabet does not write the difference

pharyngeal fricatives /ħ ʕ/ in Arabic loans and, in many dialects, in some native words (heft 'seven' with [ħ]); written h, or not at all, in the standard spelling (optional letters ḧ and an apostrophe exist)
pharyngealised (emphatic) consonants such as [sˤ tˤ zˤ] in a limited set of words in many dialects (Kahn 1976); they lower and back the neighbouring vowels and are not written
tap /ɾ/ versus trill /r/ (written r and rr); word-initial r is always the trill
five long, peripheral vowels /iː eː ɑː oː uː/ (written î ê a o û) against three short, lax vowels /ɪ ɛ ʊ/ (written i e u)
uvular stop /q/ versus velar /k/; fricatives /x ɣ/ (ɣ written x, or ẍ in some spellings)
allophony: /ɪ/ is a short centralised vowel, [ɪ] to [ɨ], and is the vowel inserted to break up consonant clusters
/ɛ/ ranges from [ɛ] to [æ] and is lowered and backed next to pharyngeals and emphatics
/ʊ/ is short and often centralised or fronted, [ʊ] to [ʉ] or [ɵ]
/k ɡ/ are fronted or palatalised before front vowels in many dialects
xw is a labialised fricative [xʷ] (xwe, xwarin)
/w/ is fronted to [ɥ] before the close front vowels /iː eː/
the unaspirated voiceless stops are tense; in some dialects they are weakly pharyngealised or glottalised
/h/ is replaced by /ħ/ in a number of words depending on dialect
vowel plus glide sequences (ew, ey, aw, ay) are not unit diphthongs
phonotactics: initial clusters are limited; many are broken up by a short [ɪ] in careful speech (bɪɾɑː or bɾɑː 'brother')
final clusters of two consonants are common (-st, -nd, -rd, -ft, -ʃt)
short /ɪ/ is unstable and drops when a suffix adds a syllable
vowel hiatus is filled by the glide [j] (written y)
the trill is the only rhotic word-initially; tap and trill contrast between vowels and word-finally

stress.type: fixed on the end of the stem; morphologically conditioned, not contrastive in the lexicon
stress.rule: Stress falls on the last syllable of the stem; inflectional endings and clitics (case endings, ezafe, indefinite -ek, personal endings, copula) are unstressed; the negative prefixes na-, ne-, ni- and the subjunctive or imperative prefix bi- take the stress; vocatives are stressed on the first syllable.
stress.cues: pitch and intensity with some lengthening; short vowels stay short under stress

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: short /ɪ/ is weakened or dropped in unstressed open syllables; the long vowels keep their quality and length
rhythm.notes: No instrumental rhythm study of Kurmanji is cited here, so the class is left as mixed. The strong difference between long and short vowels and the loss of unstressed /ɪ/ are the main timing facts.

length.notes: The long and short vowel sets differ in both duration and quality; no long vowel has a short partner of the same quality. Written rr is a trill, not a long tap. Gemination is otherwise not contrastive in the standard language.

intonation.declarative: rising accents on stressed syllables of non-final words, final fall to low
intonation.yes_no_question: word order of the statement with a final rise; an initial question particle (ma, gelo) is optional
intonation.wh_question: question word stays in place and carries the main accent; the utterance ends with a fall
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of a non-final phrase or clause
intonation.accent_shape: rise onto the stressed, stem-final syllable
intonation.notes: Instrumental work on Kurmanji intonation is sparse; this follows the reference grammars.

phonation: pharyngealisation on emphatic consonants and the vowels next to them, in a limited set of words

problems: no aspiration contrast: every voiceless stop is the unaspirated base2 p, t, k; the table defines an aspirated p# but no rule uses it, and ku_list (letters and numbers only) has no entries that could supply the aspiration the spelling leaves out
no pharyngeals /ħ ʕ/ and no emphatics: h is always [h], and an apostrophe for /ʕ/ is ignored ('erd and erd both give [ɛrd]); the optional letters ḧ and ẍ are not in ku_rules
no /ɣ/: x is always the voiceless fricative

the oblique plural ending -an is stressed (malan gives [malˈan]) although the other inflectional endings -a, -ê, -ên are correctly left unstressed; personal endings of verbs are stressed too (dibêjim gives [dˌɪbeʒˈɪm])
r is a tap only between vowels and a trill everywhere else, so word-final r and rr are both trills
good: eight vowel qualities with long and short durations (long 180 to 220, short 110 to 150 in table units)
stem-final stress (last syllable before explicitly unstressed endings), with ezafe and case endings -a, -ê, -ên unstressed
word-initial trill, tap between vowels, and the xw sequence
k and g are fronted to palatal stops before î, ê, ew and ey

notes: The eSpeak NG voice reads the Latin (Hawar) spelling only; Kurdish in Arabic script (Sorani, or Kurmanji as written in Iraq) is not covered. Aspiration, the pharyngeals and the emphatics cannot be recovered from the standard spelling without a lexicon.
